name: Cyclic glycine-proline (cGP)

lead: Cyclic glycine-proline is a small peptide the body makes from IGF-1 and that is also found in foods like blackcurrant.
People take it as a supplement for IGF-1 regulation and healthy aging.

paras: It binds IGFBP-3, which changes how much IGF-1 is freely available.
Human data are limited to small studies; reported research is mostly in animals.

angle.text: Users take it hoping to support IGF-1 function with age, which they associate with overall vitality and a younger-looking state.

lead: Cyclic glycine-proline (cGP) is a small cyclic dipeptide that the body forms as a metabolite of IGF-1, and that also occurs in some foods and marine organisms [1][2]. It is sold as a supplement by people interested in healthy-aging and IGF-1 function.

cGP binds IGF binding protein-3 and so influences how much IGF-1 is available in circulation [3][4]. People who use it connect IGF-1 function with the tissues that shape appearance with age, including skin, body composition and general vitality, and they take cGP hoping to keep IGF-1 signalling balanced as they get older.

The published research on cGP comes mainly from one academic group studying IGF-1 biology, and covers lab work, animal models, observational patient studies and one small supplementation study. Reviews describe cGP as a naturally occurring molecule with drug-like properties, and as a candidate in neurological research [5][1][3].

paras: cGP is built from the amino acids glycine and proline joined in a ring. It is thought to arise from glycine-proline-glutamate (GPE), a tripeptide cleaved from the N-terminal end of IGF-1, and a review of IGF-1-derived neuropeptides describes both GPE and cGP as natural IGF-1 metabolites [5][6]. A 2024 review describes cGP as a widespread cyclic dipeptide with a pyrrolidine-2,5-dione scaffold, found in marine organisms, produced endogenously and made synthetically [1].

Beyond the body's own production, cGP has been measured in blackcurrant anthocyanin supplements [2] and in cultures of mangrove-derived Penicillium and Aspergillus fungi, where an analytical method was developed to quantify it [7].

The best-known cGP research comes from Dr Jian Guan's group at the University of Auckland, whose 2014 Scientific Reports paper described cGP as a metabolite of IGF-1 and reported that it altered the binding of IGFBP-3 to IGF-1.[4] That paper summarised earlier work from the group showing that cGP improved recovery from ischaemic brain injury in rats and inhibited the growth of lymphoma tumours in mice, and reported cell-culture work suggesting cGP promoted IGF-1 activity when it was insufficient and inhibited it when it was excessive.[4] A 2015 review placed cGP and GPE among IGF-1-derived neuropeptides as candidates for neurological disorders.[5]

A 2022 New Zealand trade-press article describes Dr Guan's work on blackcurrants from the Canterbury region, which it says are naturally high in cGP, and a cGP supplement product named cGPMax; the article says a clinical trial in patients with type 2 diabetes and metabolic syndromes at a university-affiliated hospital in China was about to begin, and describes consumer use of concentrated cGP as early.[8] Dr Guan was quoted as saying a successful trial was expected to create more export opportunities in Asian markets.[8]

sections.h: Use in looksmaxxing and longevity circles
paras: cGP is discussed mostly in healthy-aging and nootropic contexts, as an oral supplement meant to support IGF-1 function. People who take it generally reason that IGF-1 activity declines with age and that keeping it in balance supports vitality, recovery and a younger-looking state. Reviewers of the academic literature frame the same idea in clinical terms, noting that IGF-1 function declines with age [3].

It is positioned as a milder, orally taken alternative to approaches that raise IGF-1 directly, because it acts on IGF-1 availability rather than supplying IGF-1 itself. The reviews note that exogenous IGF-1 has a large molecular size and mitogenic potential, which limits its clinical use, and that small neuropeptides were proposed as options with a more practical profile [5].

Trade coverage describes it as an early-stage, naturally derived product, and researchers describe the molecule's effects as a regulation of IGF-1 availability, which the 2014 paper called a novel mechanism of auto-regulation with potential pharmacological utility.[8][4]

IGF-1 circulates largely bound to IGFBP-3, and the reversible binding sets how much IGF-1 is free and functional. cGP retains affinity for IGFBP-3 and competes with IGF-1 for that binding, so cGP and IGFBP-3 together regulate IGF-1 bioavailability [3][4]. In the original 2014 study, the researchers reported that cGP can normalise IGF-1 function, noting that insufficient IGF-1 is associated with poor wound recovery while excess IGF-1 contributes to tumour growth [4][9].

The cGP/IGF-1 molar ratio has been proposed as a measure of functional IGF-1 [3]. The authors of the 2023 review state that the ratio is low in patients with age-related conditions such as hypertension, stroke and cognitive impairment [3].

In the blackcurrant study, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) cGP correlated with plasma cGP, and the CSF-to-plasma ratio was high for cGP and low for IGF-1 and IGFBP-3, which the authors interpreted as central uptake of plasma cGP [2].

Reviews describe neuroprotective effects of IGF-1 derived peptides in animal models [5]. In obese rats, cGP lowered systolic blood pressure and retroperitoneal fat weight, without an effect on total body composition measures reported in the abstract [10]. In a related rat study, cGP normalised a high-fat-diet-induced change in synaptic protein expression [11]. In a mouse model of Alzheimer's disease it improved memory and reduced plaque load [6]. Administration during infancy was reported to improve adult spatial memory in rats [12], and maternal administration raised IGF-1 bioavailability and novelty recognition in offspring [13].

Observational work found that stroke patients with higher plasma cGP/IGF-1 ratios had better outcomes [14]. Other human reports examined IGF-1-related growth factors in breast milk and infant weight, and cGP in pregnancy-related weight change, which are research areas on the periphery of cGP itself [15][16].

In the 2020 obese-rat study, high-fat feeding raised blood pressure, fat mass, retroperitoneal fat weight and fasting insulin and cGP while lowering IGF-1 and IGFBP-3; cGP treatment from weeks 11 to 15 reduced systolic blood pressure and retroperitoneal fat weight but did not change DEXA body composition or plasma insulin.[10] The authors suggested therapeutic potential in diet-associated cardio-metabolic complications.[10] In the 2023 APP/PS1 mouse study, cGP improved spatial memory and reduced amyloid plaque burden.[6]

In a 2019 observational study, 34 patients were recruited within three days of stroke and compared with 50 age-matched controls; baseline cGP, IGFBP-3 and the cGP/IGF-1 ratio were lower in the stroke group, and the baseline ratio correlated with neurological scores at day 90, leading the authors to propose it as a prognostic biomarker for stroke recovery.[14] The 2023 review reports that elderly people with more cGP have better memory retention and that the ratio falls with age in dementia in Parkinson disease.[3]

A trial in 11 men with Parkinson disease found that 28 days of blackcurrant anthocyanin supplementation raised cerebrospinal fluid cGP (p<0.01) without changing CSF IGF-1 or IGFBP-3; cGP was present in the supplement itself [2]. Patient studies of the cGP/IGF-1 ratio are observational, including a study of 34 stroke patients linking higher ratios to better clinical outcome [3][14]. No trials of cGP as a stand-alone supplement for appearance were found.

Reviewers describe cGP as having drug-like properties and an encouraging safety profile in the research done so far [1]. Human data on long-term oral supplementation are limited to small studies, and most reported effects come from animal experiments [5][10][6].

timeline.event: A Scientific Reports paper reports that cGP regulates IGF-1 homeostasis by altering IGFBP-3 binding to IGF-1 [4].
A review discusses IGF-1 derived neuropeptides, including cGP, as neuroprotective candidates [5].
Blackcurrant anthocyanin supplementation in Parkinson patients is reported to raise CSF cGP [2].
Plasma cGP/IGF-1 ratio is reported to predict outcome in stroke patients [14].
A review proposes cGP as a normaliser of IGF-1 function in the ageing brain, and a mouse study reports improved memory in an Alzheimer model [3][6].
A review of the marine cyclic dipeptide cGP summarises its sources and biological functions [1].
